title: Round Trip Fuel Calculator: Return Trip Fuel
description: Double a one-way distance and estimate the full round trip's fuel with the Round Trip Fuel Calculator — gallons or litres. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a 212-mile one-way trip at 31 mpg needs 6.8 gallons to get there — and 13.7 gallons for the whole round trip, the figure the tank plan needs.
quick_answer: The Round Trip Fuel Calculator doubles a one-way distance and applies your fuel consumption to estimate the complete return journey's fuel. Enter the one-way distance and the economy figure and read the round-trip fuel — because tanks, budgets and passengers' splits all belong to the whole journey, not the half.

popular_table.note: Detours and diversions add real miles the doubling cannot foresee — the calculator offers a detour allowance for exactly that honesty.

faq: Does it include detours?
You can add a detour allowance on top of the doubled distance — real journeys include the scenic error and the closed road. Without one, the figure is the clean route's fuel.
Is traffic included?
Not separately — your real-world economy figure already contains your traffic pattern. Enter the honest mpg.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. This is quantity arithmetic over a doubled distance.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Double the road one-way distance — fuel follows the wheels both ways.
Can route results change over time?
Your economy figure drifts with load and season; the return leg with a roof box is not the outbound's equal. Recompute for the loaded case.
What if the return is a different route?
Enter the average of the two one-ways as the 'one-way' distance — the doubling then prices the asymmetric round honestly.
Gallons or litres?
Both habits are served: miles/mpg here, and the Liters Needed tool for km and L/100 km.
Roof box on the return only.
Use the worse economy for the round figure or average the two legs' economies — the honest estimate sits between the two one-way answers.
I only know the round-trip distance.
Halve it for the one-way input — the doubling inside restores it, with the detour allowance still available.
Does the empty return really burn the same?
Slightly less, usually — but planning on the symmetric figure errs on the survivable side.
